display_title: Official Review of Paper359 by Reviewer s4qP

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies how to transfer robustness to the target domain, and provide light theory regarding guarantees in l-infinity norm under single-layer neural networks. The guarantee for multiple layers NN is by randomized smoothing.
content.main_review:
The paper is clearly written. 

However, this paper lacks novelty. First, transfer robustness has been extensively studied, for instance in Shafhi et al. cited by the authors. Meanwhile, using Lipchitz constrained NN to improve robustness is also a well-studied topic. The theoretical guarantee for one layer classifier is quite trivial and for multiple layers NN, using randomized smoothing can only guarantee certified robustness and also has been proposed by Cohan et al. a long time ago.

I really did not see anything novel or theoretical challenging in this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given lack of novelty, I do not think this paper is ready to be published.

content.comment:
Dear Reviewer s4qP, 

Thank you for the feedback. 

Shafahi et al. neither considered a fixed Lipschitz constant in their analysis nor used any verification technique to analyze or improve robustness.
 
Combining Lipschitz constrained neural networks with randomized smoothing techniques has not been analyzed before. Especially, there is no analysis on transfer learning models and how the property „robustness“ certifiably can be preserved during the transfer from source to target domain. We believe that rigorously studying robustness in this novel context is an important contribution in itself.

display_title: Official Review of Paper359 by Reviewer P2hQ

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed building provably robust models on target datasets by smoothing the feature extractor (on the source dataset), and using a 1-Lipschitz constrained classifier to obtain certified predictions on the target dataset. The paper argues that this gives better guarantees than smoothing the full model on the target dataset. The paper conducted experiments on various transfer tasks to verify their claims.
content.main_review:
### Strengthes:
+ The introduced method is sound and novel. The paper studies the problem of guaranteeing transfer of robustness from the source task to the target task for the first time.
+ The paper includes details about the experimental setup.

### Weaknesses:
+ The paper is not very well written and can be improved a lot. It was hard to follow.
+ The presentation of some results is confusing. For example, I am not sure what the takeaways of Table 1 and 2 are even after reading the text.
+ I found some key parts of the paper confusing. I understand that the paper is trying to sell provable transfer as an alternative for empirically transferring the robustness since we cannot really guarantee the latter. But what I don’t understand is what is being presented in S4. I think S4 is trying to argue that: “combining a fixed Lipschitz constant with adversarial training is not strong enough to make this transfer learning framework sufficiently robust.” So is it about the weakness of empirical defenses? Or about them not guaranteeing any robustness?
+ The considered transfer tasks are toy tasks. I wonder why more practical transfer tasks such as ImageNet to CIFAR10 were not conducted? The introduced method relies on randomized smoothing of the pretrained model, which has been shown to easily scale to ImageNet in Cohen et al. and follow up work.

### Detailed comments and questions:
+ It is not clear what the setting in Table 1 is. Is it a robust transfer setting? Or standard transfer? What is “WN”? (Okay I can see WN is defined in the following paragraph. I think it is useful to add it to the caption of the table too)
+ I found S4 to be really confusing (see my above comment). In addition to what I have mentioned above, I have the following questions. When you are checking if a representation is reachable from the input space, do you constrain the input to be within a bounded region around the clean datapoint? Otherwise even if you find an input that maps to the “adversarial feature”, this input is not adversarial as it might be “far” from the clean input. So I don’t understand what benefit the Lipschitz classifier is giving you is the backbone does not give guarantees?
+ In S5, it seems that if you smooth the feature representation and then “propagate the guarantees” to the Lipschitz classifier, you obtain better guarantees than smoothing the whole model on the target dataset right? So does this mean that doing this two step verification process on a non-transfer task (e.g. ImageNet to ImageNet) will give better results than randomized smoothing applied directly on the full ImageNet model?

### Small fixes:
+ Last sentence in S3: f(h(.)) -> h(f(.))
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while I think the idea is novel and potentially gives insights into how to make transfer learning probably maintain robustness, the current state of the paper is not yet ready for publication in my opinion. I would encourage the authors to improve the presentation of the paper, and address the above questions I asked.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper359 by Reviewer P2hQ

content.title: Answer to reviewer P2hQ
content.comment:
Dear reviewer P2hQ, 

Thank you for the feedback and the detailed comments. 

Q1: I am not sure what the takeaways of Table 1 [...] are.  It is not clear what the setting in Table 1 is. Is it a robust transfer setting? Or standard transfer?

A1: As discussed in the text, Table 1 shows that multi-layer classifiers achieve higher accuracy than one layer-classifiers, especially on more complex or distant transfer learning tasks. Furthermore, we wanted to show that constraining the classifier does not have a negative effect on accuracy. To this end we report accuracy on the source domain and the target domain using four transfer learning tasks of different relatedness. We will try to make the setting more clear by adding an explanation to the caption. 

Q2: I am not sure what the takeaways of Table [...] 2 are. When you are checking if a representation is reachable from the input space, do you constrain the input to be within a bounded region around the clean data point.

A2: Table 2 shows that 1-layer classifiers are not robust. [1] claimed that using transfer learning models with a 1-layer classifier improves robustness. However, the linear mapping defined by the weights and the bias can map close features/representations to very distant outputs since the weights of a one-layer classifier can (theoretically) be arbitrarily large. To illustrate this, we showed that adversarial features/representations can indeed be found for any input. In the next step, we wanted to show that such adversarial representations are reachable from the input space. We did not bound the region around the clean data, but report the distance, which is usually very close. A complementary (and simpler) approach to showing the lack of robustness is with standard attacks that directly find adversarial inputs. We will include this in the update. 

Q3: I found S4 to be really confusing. So is it about the weakness of empirical defenses?

A3: Adversarial training improves robustness but usually this defence can easily be broken by using a different attack type for robustness analysis than for training. To avoid this, certifably robust models are required. 

Q4: In S5, it seems that if you smooth the feature representation and then propagate the guarantees to the Lipschitz classifier you obtain better guarantees than smoothing the whole model on the target dataset right? So does this mean that doing this two step verification process on a non-transfer task (e.g. ImageNet to ImageNet) will give better results than randomized smoothing applied directly on the full ImageNet model? 

A2: This is something we need to investigate. Our preliminary results show that this is true (see results on the target domain in Table 3). However, since the inequality in Eq. 1 is wrong (as pointed out by reviewer tuuq) we need to re-run the experiments to confirm this finding.

[1] A. Shafahi, P. Saadatpanah, C. Zhu, A. Ghiasi, C. Studer, D. Jacobs, T. Goldstein „Adversarially Robust Transfer Learning“, ICLR 2020.

display_title: Official Review of Paper359 by Reviewer tuuq

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper analyzes whether transfer learning can be made provably robust. The paper attempts to achieve provable robustness guarantees on the transfer-target domain by controlling the Lipschitz constant of the last few layers of the network (the layers after the pre-trained feature extractor).
content.main_review:
The authors propose using a new classifier after the pre-trained feature extractor that has a controlled Lipschitz constant. This is similar to prior works that the authors mention, but the authors use L_infinity normalization instead of spectral normalization or orthonormal weight matrices. The authors claim that this alleviates some of the problems associated with the prior approaches.

However, I am quite confused, either by the writing (maybe there are key typos) or the math. In particular, I think some of the equations in the paper are incorrect as they are written. First, inequality 1 is not a proper application of Cauchy-Schwarz; the left-hand-side should be an inner product, and the L_infinity norm is not an inner product. As written right now, I think there are very simple counterexamples to inequality (1), which seems to be a key component of the rest of the analysis in the paper (it directly leads to inequality 2, which is used to justify why L_inf normalization ensures Lipschitz-ness and therefore robustness). Here is the counterexample: set W^(T(i)) = [2 1; 2 1] and (z’-z) = [2, 1]. Then the LHS has L_inf norm 5, whereas the RHS is 4, and we get 5 <= 4. Perhaps the authors meant to change some of the L_inf norms to L_1/L_2 norms or other norms?

Further along in the paper, the authors suggest a two-step process for finding adversarial inputs. I also would like to know, why do we first find an adversarial representation, then find an input matching that representation, rather than performing a search for an adversarial input directly?

Later, in Table 2, is the column p_z always going to equal 100 if you are trying to find adversarial representations? After all, it seems like any distance change is allowed, and is indeed measured in the next column.

I do appreciate that the authors did extensive experiments. With that said, I was confused about the setup of using a multi-layer classifier vs. a 1-layer classifier at the end. Perhaps investigating this avenue further could also be fruitful, as the 4-layer classifier appears to result in better results even for standard accuracy.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend a reject. The math appears incorrect/unclear, and I am also unsure of what the main takeaways/conclusions are as a result.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper359 by Reviewer tuuq

content.title: Answer to reviewer tuuq
content.comment:
Dear reviewer tuuq, 

Thank you for the feedback and the detailed comments. 

You are right, inequality 1 holds for the L_2-norm, but not for the L_inf norm. In order to ensure that a linear mapping (defined by weights W) is 1-Lipschitz we need ||Wx||_p <= ||x||_p for any x. This is equivalent to make sure that the matrix p-norm, i.e. ||W||_p = sup_{||x||_p=1} ||Wx||_p is at most 1 (see also [1] for reference). We made a last-minute switch from L2-norm to Linf-norm and missed to control inequality 1. Thank you for the hint, we will correct this. 

We searched for adversarial representations since [2] claimed that using transfer learning models with a 1-layer classifier improves robustness. However, the linear mapping defined by the weights and the bias can map close features/representations to very distant outputs since the weights of a one-layer classifier can (theoretically) be arbitrarily large. To illustrate this, we showed that adversarial features/representations can indeed be found for any input. In the next step, we wanted to show that such adversarial representations are reachable from the input space. A complementary (and simpler) approach to showing the lack of robustness is with standard attacks that directly find adversarial inputs. We will include this in the update. 


[1] C. Anil, J. Lucas, R. Grosse, „Sorting Out Lipschitz Function Approximation“, ICML 2019. 
[2] A. Shafahi, P. Saadatpanah, C. Zhu, A. Ghiasi, C. Studer, D. Jacobs, T. Goldstein „Adversarially Robust Transfer Learning“, ICLR 2020.
